items.core: In the 2025 review summary, 7,000 steps per day was associated with lower ACM compared to 2,000 steps per day. The correlation between the two groups cannot be directly regarded as the personal intervention benefit from adding 2000 to 7000 steps.
body: Judgment: Supported but with qualifications
Effect size: HR 0.53 (abstract report) 0.46–0.60 Device measured 7000 steps vs 2000 steps per day, dose-response model
Population: Adult prospective cohort; ACM included 14 studies in this comparison; review retrieved to 2025-02-14
Design: Systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis

Limitations: Residual confounding; no age-stratified conclusions; differences in device, measurement period, and previous diseases. This time, we relied on abstract values ​​and did not review the full text table by table.
Evidence: Daily steps and health outcomes in adults: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis. — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40713949/

Reader summary: Newer research reviews continue to find that taking more daily steps is associated with a lower risk of death. Participant physical condition, equipment, and measurement methods can also affect results.
items.remember: Increase the number of steps within your own capabilities; 7,000 steps can be a progressive goal for some people, and cannot be set as a hard threshold that everyone must reach.

items.title: Brushing
items.core: The ACM HR for rarely/never brushing versus regular brushing is 1.25; cancer, COPD, and cirrhosis figures are primarily risk. The observation does not mean that starting to brush your teeth can reduce ACM by 25%, nor is it a causal effect of the toothbrush itself.
body: Judgment: Supported but with qualifications
Effect size: HR 1.25 95%CI 1.21–1.28 Rarely/never brushing vs regular brushing
Population: Chinese Prospective Study of Chronic Diseases 512,715 people, 30–79 years old
Design: Large prospective cohort
Limitations: Self-reported tooth brushing behavior; associated with smoking, poverty, pre-existing health status, and access to care.
Evidence: Associations of toothbrushing behavior with risks of vascular and nonvascular diseases in Chinese adults. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7616900/

Reader summary: A large-scale follow-up in China found that people who rarely brushed their teeth had a higher risk of death. Oral care is also associated with smoking, health conditions, and medical care.
items.remember: Maintain regular brushing with fluoride toothpaste and dental disease diagnosis and treatment; it cannot replace measures such as controlling smoking and blood pressure.

items.title: Bathing
items.core: 28%, 26%, and 46% of the original database correspond to the incidence of CVD, stroke, and cerebral hemorrhage respectively. The numbers can be verified, but they are not ACM. Finding no significant association with sudden death does not mean bathing is completely safe.
body: Judgment: No direct ACM evidence
Effect size: ACM not reported; CVD incidence HR 0.72 ACM not reported; CVD incidence 95% CI 0.62–0.84 Almost daily/daily bathing vs. 0–2 times per week
Population: 30,076 Japanese aged 40–59 years, no CVD or cancer at baseline; follow-up 1990–2009
Design: Japanese prospective cohort; endpoints were cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events

Limitations: No randomization; Japanese bathtub habits cannot be directly generalized to showering; risks such as drowning and heat stress are not excluded by the lack of significant sudden death results.
Evidence: Habitual tub bathing and risks of incident coronary heart disease and stroke. — https://europepmc.org/article/MED/32209614
Reader summary: Follow-up of middle-aged Japanese people found that frequent bathing is associated with less incidence of cardiovascular disease and stroke.
items.remember: You can bathe in warm water according to comfortable and safe habits; those with a tendency to faint, acute illness, drunkenness or cardiovascular instability should avoid long soaks in hot water and bathing alone.

items.title: Heavy housework (elderly men)
items.core: Men’s participation in heavy housework is associated with a 29% lower ACM, but 72 years old is the average age of the included sample, and the enrollment requirement is ≥65 years old; it does not have an effect after the age of 72, nor is it a trial conclusion to reduce the “average mortality rate”. Results for women were not significant.
body: Judgment: Correction required
Effect size: HR 0.71 95%CI 0.56–0.91 Participation in heavy housework vs. non-participation
Population: Elderly people aged ≥65 years old in Hong Kong community; 2867 people, average 72 years old after excluding specific chronic diseases; 452 deaths
Design: Prospective single cohort, about 9 years of follow-up

Limitations: Those who can do housework may be healthier; moving furniture/gas tanks cannot be used as a life extension prescription. The 2013 correction only corrects the proportion of male and female participation in housework in the article.
Evidence: Housework reduces all-cause and cancer mortality in Chinese men. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3647044/

Reader summary: In a follow-up of Hong Kong elderly people, men who did heavier housework had a lower risk of death, but no clear association was found in women. People with better physical fitness are better able to do housework, which may also affect the results.
items.remember: Participate in an appropriate amount of housework according to physical strength; those with frailty, osteoporosis, back problems, or risk of falls should avoid lifting heavy objects.

items.title: Sleep duration
items.core: Compared with self-reported 7 hours, the ACM of men with ≥10 hours is 34% higher and that of women is 48% higher. The numbers are consistent. Long sleeps may also reflect underlying diseases; this does not mean that long sleepers must be forced to reduce their sleep time to 7 hours, or that changing the duration will necessarily change mortality.
body: Judgment: Supported but with qualifications
Effect size: HR 1.34 for men; HR 1.48 for women, 95% CI 1.26–1.44; 1.36–1.61 respectively Self-reported ≥10 hours vs 7 hours; each cohort has two calibers: night sleep or full-day sleep including nap

Population: 9 cohorts of 322,721 people from Japan, China, Singapore, and South Korea, with an average age of 54.5; excluding baseline self-reported CVD/cancer and those who died in the 5 years before follow-up; 19,419 males and 13,768 females died
Design: Individual data combined across multiple cohorts, prospective Follow-up was about 13–14 years

Limitations: The duration was only self-reported once: most cohorts were measured at baseline, and the Shanghai Women's Health Study was measured at the third follow-up; the questionnaires for each cohort were not standardized (night sleep or full-day duration including naps); residual confounding did not capture information such as sleep quality, depression, and socioeconomics; excluding baseline CVD/cancer and death in the first 5 years still cannot completely eliminate reverse causation.
Evidence: Association of Sleep Duration With All- and Major-Cause Mortality Among Adults in Japan, China, Singapore, and Korea. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8417759/

Reader summary: Follow-up in many Asian countries found that people who sleep for a long time have a higher risk of death; longer sleep may also be a manifestation of underlying diseases or sleep problems.
items.remember: Maintain adequate, regular sleep and recover well after waking up; long-term sleep accompanied by fatigue, snoring or drowsiness should investigate the cause.

items.title: Bedtime
items.core: The original study can verify that going to bed early and late is related to adverse outcomes, but the abstract of the original paper that has been read does not provide the independent effect and CI of "ACM is 43% higher, 15% higher", and the second-hand figures cannot be copied into fully adjusted ACM. Abstract The fully adjusted results are HR1.09 and 1.10 for the composite endpoint of death + non-fatal cardiovascular events, which cannot replace pure ACM.
body: Judgment: Partial support

Effect size: ACM independent value could not be verified; composite endpoint HR 1.09/1.10 ACM not verified; composite endpoint 95%CI 1.03–1.16/1.02–1.20 About before 22 o’clock or after midnight vs going to bed from 22 o’clock to midnight
Population: 21 countries PURE 112,198 people; 9.2 years of follow-up; 5633 deaths, 5346 major cardiovascular events
Design: multinational prospective cohort; self-reported bedtime

Limitations: social schedule and disease confounding; full adjustment significantly weakens the association; the precise boundaries are slightly different in Methods and Conclusion, and are not necessarily hard thresholds.
Evidence: Association of bedtime with mortality and major cardiovascular events: an analysis of 112,198 individuals from 21 countries in the PURE study. — https://europepmc.org/article/MED/33610073

Reader summary: Cross-national follow-up found that early or late bedtime was associated with a higher composite risk of death and major cardiovascular events; the association was significantly attenuated after other factors were taken into account.
items.remember: Maintain a regular and adequate amount of sleep according to your personal rhythm; do not deliberately postpone an otherwise appropriate early bedtime because of this relationship.

items.title: Sedentary and watching TV
items.core: Higher amounts of sedentary time are associated with higher ACM, but the fixed increase of 3% per additional hour does not apply to all sedentary levels. The corresponding systematic review found a non-linear relationship: about 1% per hour in the total sedentary period ≤8 hours, and about 4% in the >8 hour interval; watching TV also has different slopes. 6-8 hours and 3-4 hours are observation model turning points, not safety lines.
body: Judgment: Partial support

Effect size: RR for each additional hour of total sedentary time 1.01 (≤8h/d); 1.04 (>8h/d) 95%CI 1.00–1.01; 1.03–1.05 respectively Increase total sitting time by 1 hour/day within the corresponding exposure interval
Population: 34 prospective studies, a total of 1,331,468 independent participants with different outcomes
Design: Systematic review, dose-response meta-analysis, adjusting physical activity

Limitations: Sitting is mostly self-reported, study heterogeneity and residual confounding; the association of cancer death in this review is not significant and cannot be mixed with cancer incidence. The original Chinese report PDF and the old WHO PDF cannot be accessed.

Evidence: Sedentary behavior and risk of all-cause, cardiovascular and cancer mortality, and incident type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and dose response meta-analysis. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6133005/

Reader Summary: A review of studies found that longer periods of sitting are associated with a higher risk of death, especially among people who sit more hours each day. The association between watching television and total sitting time also differed.
items.remember: Replace some of the prolonged sitting with walking or activities when the ability allows, and exercise regularly; those who are unable to stand should carry out activities according to rehabilitation recommendations, and no unproven uniform rest frequency is required.

items.title: Pessimism/Optimism
items.core: Original database HR1.134, etc. are consistent with the paper, which is the correlation for every 1 standard deviation increase in the pessimistic score. The lack of a significant correlation between optimism scores in this study does not mean that optimism is unhelpful; the paper's statement that reverse causation is "unlikely" does not rule it out.
body: Judgment: Supported but with qualifications
Effect size: ACM HR per 1SD pessimism score 1.134; further adjusted HR 1.160 95%CI 1.065–1.207; 1.083–1.242 respectively Every 1 standard deviation increase in pessimism score
Population: 2978 related samples of Australian twins aged ≥50 years, with an average of 1068 deaths after 20 years; specific models are reduced due to missing numbers
Design: Prospective single cohort, survival model considering family clustering
Limitations: Psychological traits are not randomly assigned; reverse causality is not ruled out; there is no direct experimental evidence that emotion therapy reduces ACM.
Evidence: Pessimism is associated with greater all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, but optimism is not protective. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7387533/

Reader's abstract: Higher pessimism scores were associated with a higher risk of death during follow-up of middle-aged and older Australians. Emotions, physical health, and life circumstances all influence each other.
items.remember: Seek support or professional help when persistent pessimism or low mood affects your life; do not replace treatment with forced optimism.

items.title: Social isolation, loneliness and living alone
items.core: In the adjusted meta-results, social isolation, loneliness and living alone were associated with death odds ratios of 1.29, 1.26 and 1.32 respectively. The three are different exposures, and the OR cannot be rewritten as HR or an increase in individual absolute mortality; it has not been proven that increasing social contact will inevitably reverse the same risk.
body: Judgment: Supported but with qualifications

Effect size: social isolation OR 1.29; loneliness OR 1.26; living alone OR 1.32 Not reported (the original abstract read did not give a 95% CI, so it was not filled in second-hand) Social isolation/loneliness/living alone vs Each study corresponds to the low exposure group
Population: death follow-up studies up to February 2014 are included; each study population and adjustment factors are different
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of original studies
Limitations: Baseline health status affects the results; heterogeneous exposure definitions; Living alone does not equal loneliness; This article is only an abstract.
Evidence: Loneliness and social isolation as risk factors for mortality: a meta-analytic review. — https://europepmc.org/article/MED/25910392

Reader summary: Research review finds that social isolation, loneliness, and living alone are all associated with a higher risk of mortality, but they are different life experiences. People who live alone can also have fulfilling and reliable connections.
items.remember: Maintain reliable contact and help-seeking channels according to personal wishes, and pay attention to hearing, mobility, depression and other disabilities; it is not required that all people living alone live together.

items.title: Net worth/economic resources
items.core: The original database sample is consistent with the direction; ACM HR0.95 for every 50,000 US dollars more in net worth, and the within-family model is 0.94, but the twin subgroup CI spans 1. It cannot be inferred that increasing wealth through specific investments prolongs life proportionally, nor is it an ecological effect of the gap between rich and poor.
body: Judgment: Supported but with qualifications

Effect size: HR 0.95 for every $50,000 increase in net worth; within-family HR 0.94 95%CI 0.94–0.97; 0.91–0.97, respectively, for every $50,000 increase in self-reported net worth from 1994 to 1996 (study unit)
Population: United States MIDUS 5414 people, average age 46.7, nearly 24 years of follow-up; 1010 deaths; 2490 siblings/twins
Design: Single cohort and intra-family comparison
Limitations: Self-reported net worth; limited ethnic representation; individual non-shared mixing, health-related wealth decline; no intervention to improve income tested.
Evidence: Association of Wealth With Longevity in US Adults at Midlife. — https://midus.wisc.edu/findings/pdfs/2366.pdf

Reader Summary: Follow-up of middle-aged Americans finds that greater net worth is associated with lower risk of death. The relationship between economic resources, health, and life security is often a two-way street.
items.remember: Prioritize stable housing, medical accessibility, and basic financial security; high-risk investments cannot be treated as health interventions.

items.title: Weight changes from early adulthood to middle age
items.core: The HR for reducing obesity to overweight is 0.46 compared to continuing to be obese, and the numbers are consistent; the HR for reducing overweight to normal is 1.12 compared to continuing to be overweight, and the CI spans 1, which means that there is no significant difference. It cannot be said that reducing to normal weight is unhelpful or harmful. Weight loss occurs between the ages of 25 and middle-aged, and is not applicable to involuntary wasting in the elderly.
body: Judgment: Supported but with qualifications
Effect size: Obesity→overweight HR 0.46; overweight→normal HR 1.12 95%CI 0.27–0.77; 0.86–1.45 respectively vs persistent obesity and persistent overweight respectively
Population: NHANES 24,205 U.S. adults aged 40–74 years; recall of weight at age 25 and 10 years before baseline; 10.7 years of follow-up, 5846 deaths
Design: Observational study linking retrospective weight history to prospective mortality
Limitations: Obesity → overweight only 214; non-randomized intervention; 54% could not demonstrate causal benefit from active weight loss.
Evidence: Association of Weight Loss Between Early Adulthood and Midlife With All-Cause Mortality Risk in the US. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7428805/
Reader summary: Follow-up in the United States found that people who fell from obesity to overweight from early adulthood to middle age had a lower risk of death than those who remained obese.
items.remember: Obese people and medical staff should formulate long-term weight and muscle strength management; those who are elderly, pregnant or involuntarily lose weight should not follow the weight loss conclusion.

items.title: Waist circumference and abdominal obesity
items.core: A prospective cohort summary of adults found that every 10 cm increase in waist circumference was associated with an approximately 11% higher risk of all-cause mortality. After taking BMI into account, abdominal fat measures still provide additional risk information.
body: Judgment: Supported but with qualifications
Effect size: HR 1.11 per 10 cm increase in waist circumference 95%CI 1.08–1.13 per 10 cm increase in waist circumference; comparing adults with different waist circumferences
Population: 72 prospective cohorts, 2,528,297 people reviewed; waist circumference analysis included 50 studies
Design: Systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective cohorts

Limitations: The heterogeneity among studies is high; waist circumference measurement methods, underlying diseases and lifestyles are different. Waist circumference is a risk indicator, not a directly measured visceral fat mass; this conclusion does not set a unified weight loss target.
Evidence: Central fatness and risk of all cause mortality: systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of 72 prospective cohort studies. — https://www.bmj.com/content/370/bmj.m3324

Reader summary: In addition to weight, waist circumference is also worth paying attention to. Multiple long-term studies have found that the larger the waist circumference, the higher the risk of all-cause mortality; looking only at weight may miss the risk of abdominal fat.
items.remember: In addition to weight, also pay attention to long-term changes in waist circumference; when abdominal fat increases, gradually improve it based on diet, exercise and health assessment.

items.title: New Crown Epidemic and All-Cause Excess Deaths
items.core: The original paper supports all-cause excess deaths in the first wave of the epidemic, but the 21 countries are 19 European countries plus Australia and New Zealand, excluding the United States. It cannot support the original database's "US COVID-19 mortality rate 1.5%" or "average life expectancy reduced by 2 years"; the former still lacks time, denominator and case/infection mortality definitions. Excess deaths from the epidemic also include indirect effects such as medical interruptions.
body: Judgment: Correction required

Effect size: 206,000 excess deaths in 21 countries from mid-February to the end of May 2020; non-individual HR 95% Bayesian confidence interval 178,100–231,000; non-95%CI actual all-cause death vs Epidemic-free counterfactual model prediction
Population: National death registration in 21 industrialized countries, first wave in 2020; excluding the United States
Design: Population time series/ecological study of 16 Bayesian model ensembles

Limitations: Counterfactual model and registration delay; 2020 scenario cannot extrapolate current variant strains, immunity and medical conditions; the original link to the CDC is a general death data entry and does not directly support the original number.

Evidence: Magnitude, demographics and dynamics of the effect of the first wave of the COVID-19 pandemic on all-cause mortality in 21 industrialized countries. — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-020-1112-0.pdf

Reader summary: Death registrations in many countries show that there were significant excess deaths during the first wave of the COVID-19 pandemic, including both infections and indirect effects such as medical interruptions. This reflects the epidemic environment at that time.
items.remember: Reduce infection exposure, ensure basic diseases and timely medical management; specific protection and treatment are based on current applicable guidelines, and no fixed percentage of 2020 is used to estimate individual risks.

items.title: Obstructive sleep apnea
items.core: In a summary of prospective observational studies, severe obstructive sleep apnea is associated with a higher risk of all-cause mortality. In the 2025 Treatment Review, a summary of randomized trials of positive airway pressure therapy did not show a clear reduction in ACM, and a lower risk was observed in nonrandomized studies.
body: Judgment: Supported but with qualifications
Effect size: Severe vs. no sleep apnea: HR 1.90 95% CI 1.29–2.81 Severe obstructive sleep apnea vs. no disease; not treated vs. no treatment
Population: Risk review 6 prospective observational studies, 11,932 people; grouped by apnea severity
Design: Meta-analysis of prospective observational studies; also refer to the comprehensive study of positive airway pressure therapy

Limitations: Underlying disease and treatment selection may affect the results; the treatment review mixed randomized and non-randomized studies, and the comprehensive results cannot be considered as randomized trial evidence. Snoring itself does not equal a diagnosis.
Evidence: Is obstructive sleep apnea associated with cardiovascular and all-cause mortality? — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23936014/

Reader summary: If you sleep long, you may not sleep well. Severe sleep apnea is associated with a higher risk of death, and chronic snoring, breath holding, and daytime sleepiness deserve to be investigated.
items.remember: If you snore loudly for a long time, hold your breath while sleeping, or always feel sleepy during the day, do a sleep assessment; after diagnosis, choose treatment with your doctor.
